summary.title: The Same-Origin Policy (500 Lines or Less, Alloy model)
summary.one_liner: You learn what the same-origin policy protects against and how to model browsers, HTTP, DNS and client-side scripts as an executable Alloy model to reason about it.
keywords: how does the same-origin policy work
takeaways: The same-origin policy restricts when scripts in a browser can communicate, and it guards against attacks such as reading private data or emptying bank accounts.
The SOP is both too restrictive (blocking legitimate mashups) and not restrictive enough (leaving CSRF-style holes).
Alloy models are not run like programs; the analyzer simulates instances and checks properties within a bounded scope, generating test cases automatically.
The model abstracts HTTP as RPC-like calls and assumes static DNS, so it cannot capture every vulnerability.
summary.summary: This chapter from the 500 Lines or Less book explains the same-origin policy (SOP), the browser mechanism controlling cross-script communication, and builds an executable Alloy model of it. It incrementally models URLs, clients, servers, DNS, cookies, HTTP requests, browsers, documents and scripts, using run and check commands to generate instances and find counterexamples. The authors note the model simplifies aspects such as response ordering and DNS changes. The page then previews four techniques for bypassing SOP restrictions, which are not covered in this excerpt.
